DecSummary: An office worker did not have entitlement for carpal tunnel syndrome. The condition was not a disablement from the nature of her work. The worker's duties were not forceful or repetitive in the sense described in the Tribunal discussion paper on carpal tunnel syndrome. There was periodic stapling, which involved some modest amount of force, but was not of a continuous nature. Keyboarding was one of her main duties but even that was broken up by regular changes of tasks and, in any event, keyboarding has not been persuasively shown to be a cause of carpal tunnel syndrome. A supportive ergonomic analysis, which was based on only an interview with the worker, was not persuasive because it was based on inadequate and inaccurate information.

The worker's application for reconsideration of Decision No. 3205/16 was denied. There was no error in finding that the worker had voluntarily under-employed herself by moving, after the accident, from a larger urban centre to a smaller community with fewer employment opportunities. The Vice-Chair rejected the worker's submission that she was forced to move in order to secure affordable child care so that she could complete her college program. Regardless of the merits and motivation, the move was a choice made by the worker. In any event, there was no evidence to establish that the move was necessary so that the worker could complete her studies and, even if it was necessary, there was no evidence why she could not have moved back to an area of higher employment after completing her studies.

The worker's application for reconsideration of Decision No. 1210/16 was granted with regard to one of the issues on the appeal. That issue related to temporary total disability benefits from July 1994 to August 1995. The worker had claimed that he was actively involved in physiotherapy. The original decision found that he was not, based on an analysis of OHIP billing records (which did not include the physiotherapist) and clinical notes of the family doctor. However, the decision failed to deal with the oral evidence of the worker, who testified that he had numerous physiotherapy treatments per week. This was consistent with OHIP billing records that showed 245 visits to the worker's doctor during the period in question. The doctor's clinical notes indicated only 21 visits. New submissions on this application for reconsideration asserted that the physiotherapist was associated with the office of the doctor and that the physiotherapist billed for the treatments through the officer of the doctor.
